entries.title: Did an AI Music App Just Snitch on the Song of the Summer?
entries.summary: Fenix Flexin’s hit song “Rubberz” has hip-hop fans arguing over whether it was generated by AI. Some say they have proof it’s machine-made, but will anyone care?
entries.content:
There is no such thing as a universal “song of the summer” anymore, but if you’re into rap music, Fenix Flexin’s “Rubberz” is a pretty strong contender.

Officially released in June, it currently sits at No. 58 in the Billboard Hot 100 and has a music video with 7 million views. Lyrically, it’s got everything you’d want: boasts about cash and jewelry, and bars that work as a double entendre for braggadocio and depression.

But there are two interesting twists to “Rubberz.” First, it isn’t a rap song at all; it’s a synth-pop tune that would be at home in a moody ’80s playlist. Also, since it dropped, it’s been the focus of accusations that it was completely or partially AI-generated.

The argument reached a peak this weekend after an independent music producer claimed he’d figured out not only how Fenix had made “Rubberz” but that the rapper’s labelmate, Tyga, also seems to have used a little-known generative AI music app to create some ’80s-themed tunes of his own.

And now, the creators of that same AI music app have effectively snitched on both: The service’s new built-in detector is now flagging the songs made by both Fenix and Tyga as likely AI-generated.

This may finally settle the argument fans have been having all summer. It won’t settle the one they’re about to start.

Tune Up

People were suspicious of Fenix from the beginning; “Rubberz” is not only an unusual genre shift for the artist, it also doesn’t sound like his voice in the song.

Fenix Flexin grew up in East Hollywood, and he sounds like it, and when he debuted as part of the group Shoreline Mafia in the late 2010s, you could always recognize which bars were his because of his somewhat nasally, congested voice. The voice on his June 5 release of “Rubberz,” however, is completely unrecognizable. It’s a lot brighter and crisper, and the accent sounds closer to a very chipper Morrissey.

Both he and the credited producer, Purps on the Beat, have denied using AI at every turn. Fenix told Channel 5 that he “freestyled” the lyrics, and in the comments of an On the Radar performance, he replied to people accusing him of using AI: "No sirrrrrrr, recorded same as all music I do! Only difference is auto-tune reverb and me using my fake uk accent lol."

Not everyone bought his explanation, but there was no proof otherwise. As the summer continued, music media debated whether “Rubberz” had been AI-generated. But none of the well-known AI music detectors flagged it, Fenix denied it, and the song continued to rack up plays. Fans had no choice but to get comfortable with the question being unresolved.

Then, things shifted suddenly. On Thursday, a music producer named Medasin posted a video claiming he’d figured out how Fenix used AI to make the track.

It wasn’t Suno, or Udio, the two most prominent generative AI tools for making music. Instead, Medasin says, Flexin had used a lesser-known app called Treblo. Medasin breaks down his accusation methodically: First, he points out that the app used to be called Sonauto until two days before “Rubberz” was released. And then he shows a screen cap of one of Fenix’s old Instagram Stories teasing his new ’80s sound. A freeze-frame and zoom reveals that a filename being shown on screen has the suffix “Sonauto.mp3.”

But the most compelling accusation comes when Medasin shows how he was able to use Treblo to create a very similar track. By using tags like “80s synthwave” and prompting the app to write lyrics about a “rapper lifestyle,” Medasin got a similar-sounding song. The lyrics even bear more than a passing resemblance to “Rubberz.”

For example, Medasin’s prompt got him the lyrics “Diamond chains hanging heavy”; “Rubberz” has “Now I bought a heavy diamond chain.” Medasin’s generated song gave him “I see your face in the champagne bubbles”; Fenix’ song has “Still seeing your face in the glass.” Both songs feature some permutation of “pockets thick,” both mention “plastic smiles.”

“There's just way too many coincidences,” Medasin said in an interview with WIRED. “It is just a mathematical impossibility that he did not use Treblo.”

This all made me curious, though. Would Treblo allow me to re-create a “Rubberz”-style song? It turns out: yes.

By entering tags like “80s synthwave” and asking it to make rap lyrics, I got not only a similar sound but similar lyrical structures.

In my first try, I generated a song (you can hear it here) with the couplet “Rings on every finger / Leather seats and cedar scent linger,” an almost mirror duplicate of the “Rubberz” line “Gold rings on my fingers / Still your perfume lingers.” I continued to generate songs. Even with slight variations, any time I combined an “80s” tag with a prompt for “rap lyrics,” I got similar results.

Whereas ChatGPT seems to like goblins, em dashes, and “it’s not X, it’s Y” constructions, Treblo’s engine seems to be obsessed with “finger/linger” rhyme pairs, talking about rings and glass and pockets, and song constructions in which there is a thematic transition from night into day.

Medasin says his Treblo revelation happened a month ago, but he kept it quiet; he figured some journalist would do the legwork of connecting the dots for the public. This did happen on a smaller scale, perhaps most thoroughly on an AI music news site called Zinstrel, but it never really broke through. Medasin’s video was the first to capture attention.

As Thursday went on, it seemed that Medasin had struck a nerve with his video accusation. That afternoon, Fenix posted a video on his Instagram page of what he said was the original project file for “Rubberz.” If authentic, this would serve as proof that the song was not AI; that “Rubberz” had been created from scratch in a studio.

But music producers immediately jumped into the comments, with many claiming that the project file being shown looked suspiciously like someone had just taken an existing song and used a “stem separator” to extract a full song into rudimentary components like bass and drums; which would point back to it just being an AI song that they couldn’t create.

Hours later, Fenix deleted the post. Neither he nor Purps on the Beat have addressed the “evidence” video since, or why it was taken down. Requests for comment sent to both by WIRED went unanswered.

Then, another one. Two days later, on Saturday, Medasin dropped another video, this time alleging that Tyga’s new $TARFACE project is also at least partially using Treblo. He starts with some loose connections: videos were posted on social media of Tyga and Fenix together, both are on the same label, the same sudden rapper-to-’80s crooner pathway. But also, he ran a Tyga song in a new AI music detector a friend is developing, and it was flagged as AI.

But it’s more convincing to hear directly from Treblo itself.

"Someone appears to have used our model to find a sound that millions of people connected with,” Treblo cofounder Ryan Tremblay said when asked for comment, “and that's exciting.”

Treblo had not previously spoken to Tyga or Fenix, Tremblay says, and the company wasn’t “even aware [“Rubberz”] existed until after it hit the Hot 100.”

Asking Treblo about individual songs might not be necessary in the future. Late Sunday night, Treblo published a page titled “Was This Made With Treblo?” In short, it’s a Treblo music detector. “We also think listeners should know what they're hearing,” a blog post explains, describig it as a tool that is “tuned to detect songs made with Treblo with little to no modification.”

Sure enough, feeding “Rubberz” into the tool returns a result of “Very likely Treblo.” Running a track that Tyga dropped in early July returns a result of “Likely Treblo.”

The rate of false positives, Treblo’s site says, is under one in 10,000; a fraction of a percent. The detector’s efficacy has not been independently reviewed, but Treblo has released the code under an open source license so anyone can inspect it and test it.

Requests sent by WIRED to Tyga’s label for comment were not returned.

Slop or Not

The timing of all this coincides with a trend of platforms making gestures toward AI-generated content. The same day that Medasin posted his first video, LinkedIn rolled out a new feature: a “seems like AI” button that allows users to flag AI slop in posts. Two weeks ago, Substack released a new feature that purports to detect AI-written newsletters. Tidal has blocked monetization of AI-generated music, and while Spotify doesn’t have an AI tagging feature, there’s a crowdsourced tracker where you can report slop to other listeners.

The proliferation of image and video generators over the past few years has provoked worries about the spread of machine-made content and misinformation. A bipartisan AI Labeling Act in the US Senate has been suggested as a partial solution: forcing platforms to visibly label AI-generated content so that it would be clear whether online content is real or not. “People deserve to know,” one senator told Politico.

What we should have anticipated was that there would be people who don’t want to know. People who would get angry if you ruin the fantasy.

The comment section of Medasin’s first video is full of this: people who say they like “Rubberz” anyway, that they don’t care that the song is AI. That AI is the future and that Medasin is just jealous that Fenix thought of it first.

Medasin says he wasn’t surprised by the reaction. He admits he liked the song when he first heard it and still somewhat enjoys it in an ironic sort of way. “It's catchy, and it was stuck in my head for a fucking month,” he says. So why risk a bunch of people looking at him like he’s the guy in the conspiracy board meme?

Ultimately, Medasin says, he thinks there can be a place for AI in music, even if he doesn’t like it personally. But he wants artists to tell the truth, so listeners can decide for themselves.

“This is, like, a critical moment in music history,” Medasin tells WIRED, “and I have very, very deep respect and love for the journey of musicians and humans and human experience being celebrated and present in music.” He decries anyone who would be deceptive about that and profit off of it. “It is unethical to me on a very spiritual level,” he says.

Music fans spent half the summer arguing over whether a surprise hit song was synthetic. It looks like they have an answer. Now they just have to decide how much it matters to them.

entries.title: The SpaceX Falcon Lunar Crash Is a Warning for Moon Bases
entries.summary: The risk of more debris hitting the moon is on the rise as the space race heats up.
entries.content:
A SpaceX rocket that has been drifting in space for a year and a half is set to crash into the moon on Wednesday, stirring up a debris cloud that could be visible from Earth. The impact raises questions on the future of lunar exploration, including how to protect any future moon bases from space junk.

The rocket set for moon impact is the upper stage of a Falcon 9 that transported a pair of lunar landers. While the landers successfully reached the surface, the rocket was left adrift since it did not have enough fuel to return to Earth or enter a stable orbit.

Weighing 4 metric tons, the rocket is expected to strike the lunar surface at a speed of approximately 5,400 mph—about seven times the speed of sound. Without an atmosphere to slow the projectile down, the impact will cause an explosion equivalent to 3 metric tons of TNT, leaving a crater that’s projected to be up to 27 meters in diameter and 5 meters deep.

The upper stage is expected to hit the surface around 6:34 am UTC on Wednesday, likely making impact near Einstein Crater on the western edge of the moon’s near side. The Americas will have the best view of this impact. While it won’t be visible to the naked eye, viewers should be able to spot the debris plume through a good telescope for a few minutes.

A lunar crash landing visible from Earth will be a spectacle, one that raises concerns about the future of the moon. Multiple countries are planning uncrewed lunar missions, which could clutter the area around the moon. This SpaceX rocket won’t be the first to accidentally crash into the moon. In March 2022, a Chinese Long March 3C rocket also struck the lunar surface and left a crater that’s 29 meters wide.

China and the US are also pushing to build bases on the surface in the coming decades.

Bill Gray, the creator of the Project Pluto initiative to develop software and tools to track the orbits of asteroids, comets, and artificial satellites, was the first to calculate the trajectory of the impending Falcon 9 crash. He was also part of a team that worked on a preprint study released last month detailing the collision.

The crash landing is ”an opportunity to test pipelines for measuring flash properties to locate impact events seismically, and to better understand the multi-modal hazards posed to future lunar infrastructure and astronauts from space debris impacting the Moon,” the study states.

Although building a moon research center capable of supporting a sustained human presence will take at least a decade, NASA’s missions to construct the first facilities are expected to launch in the coming years as part of the Artemis program.

"These sorts of things are going to happen more and more often. And as we have more astronauts on the lunar surface, more lunar infrastructure habitats, for example, we need to understand how much of a risk these impact events actually pose," Benjamin Fernando, a researcher at Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico and coauthor of the preprint study, tells ABC News.

The risk posed by space debris is part of a growing list of hazards that cast doubt on the safety of any long-term project on the moon. In addition to the potential for space junk to wreak havoc on the lunar surface, natural events such as meteorite strikes also threaten any future activities. But with any potential lunar bases still a decade or more away, there’s ample time for researchers to look at the hazards and plan for them.

“This is an ideal way of studying both the direct risks, the risk of being hit by debris or being blinded by a flash of light, but also the indirect risk, the risk of being hit by a cloud of ejected material and having that disrupt or interfere with spacecraft functions in lunar orbit as well,” Fernando says.

entries.title: Best Robot Lawn Mowers (2026): My Picks After 3 Years of Testing
entries.summary: Smart mowers are an expensive alternative to old-fashioned yard work, but they’re finally good enough to consider if you’d rather sip an iced tea and watch a robot tame your lawn.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Lawn care is a monotonous, thankless task. Who wants to mow the lawn when you could be lollygagging in a hammock with a cold drink, watching a robot do it for you? That’s right: no one. Robot lawn mowers were once the preserve of the wealthy, and yes, they can still be on the pricey side. But they’re getting cheaper and better all the time.

I’ve tested a handful of the best robot lawn mowers over the past three years, and after comparing a fresh crop this mowing season, I'm delighted to tell you that robot mowers are actually good now. I've got some recommendations, honorable mentions, and a list of robot mowers you should avoid. Read on for everything you need to know about lawn-tending bots.

Updated August 2026: I added an Anthbot mower as my new budget pick. I also added details to my top pick after further testing, some information on a model I don’t recommend from Stiga, and updated prices.

Mowers I Am Currently Testing

I am testing the Sunseeker X7 Gen 2 next, and then the Eufy C15 and a Roborock mower. One of my colleagues is currently testing a Navimow.

Other Robot Mowers I Tested and Liked

With a sleek design and a mixture of 360-degree lidar for 3D mapping and a camera with AI vision, this mower proved very effective. Setup was straightforward, and there’s no need for wires or an antenna, though I did have to adjust the map manually. You can set multiple areas, and its navigation is generally very good. It mowed in neat lines, successfully avoided thin posts for the badminton net and other obstacles, and completed an excellent edge pass at the end. With some of the closest edge mowing I’ve seen, I was all set to recommend this mower, but then it got stuck. A couple of times, it seemed to be stuck, then managed to free itself, but an uneven problem spot proved to be its nemesis, and it chewed up a patch of grass trying to get free. Eventually, I had to make that spot a no-go zone. This mower is still worth considering, particularly if you see it on sale; just be prepared to tweak the map. The 2000 covers up to half an acre. If you have a quarter of an acre or less, the Mova Lidax 1000 ($1,299) is much cheaper but has the same features.

Husqvarna Aspire R6V for £999: While the reliable Husqvarna 410XE Nera was my top pick for a long time, you can get more affordable mowers now, without the hassle of RTK antennas. The Husqvarna Aspire R6V is just such a mower. It uses a combination of GPS and AI vision with a camera on the front. It was easy to set up and map the lawn in the app, but you will need a good Wi-Fi signal across your yard for it to work effectively. I was a little disappointed in the sensitive obstacle avoidance, as it left large uncut strips around the edges of my lawn. I was able to reduce the verge a little with some tinkering, but it was still larger than the recommendations above. Note: This model is currently not available in the US.

Anthbot Genie 3000 for $1,199: This often-discounted mower was my budget pick for a while, but mowers have moved on, so you can get better performance without the satellite antenna now. It offers auto-mapping, but the remote-control option works better. The mower cut my lawn effectively, but even after repeated map updates, it left an uncut verge. The obstacle avoidance works well, and it cuts in neat lines. It had no issues returning to charge or following a schedule. The voice that says it has connected or started mowing began to annoy me, but thankfully, it can be turned off. There were some glitches with rain alerts that prevented it from mowing, even long after the rain had stopped. I also experienced some flaky connection issues with the GPS, and it occasionally got stuck. While there is support for multiple areas, the mower often struggled picking up a signal in my front yard. Ultimately, this is still a decent mower when discounted, provided you have a modest-sized, straightforward lawn.

Eufy Robot Lawn Mower E15 for $1,799: This is another wire-free mower, but instead of relying on satellite navigation, it uses a camera system to automatically map lawns and avoid obstacles. It can cover up to 0.2 acres (8,700 square feet), cut from 1 to 3 inches, and handle up to 18-degree slopes. It is also fairly quiet and has GPS tracking, but you must have Wi-Fi coverage in your backyard, or you'll need a 4G data subscription. I found the setup lengthy due to a firmware download, but the mapping and the first cut were decent. The E15 can only run during the day, and it doesn't cope very well with inclines. I also found it frequently failed to cut the edges of the lawn and doesn't perform well if the grass is damp. I wouldn't recommend it at full price, but it seems to get frequent deep discounts.

Avoid These Mowers

Stiga A6V: I like that this mower only needs the charging station and has no need for an antenna. The buggy setup was my first red flag, as a firmware update failed and had to be repeated. Once up and running, I found the mower always left a big verge, even after adjustment. The AI vision camera is very slow to react to obstacles and not very good at navigating around them. It hit the ball several times in my test, and I had to hit the stop button as it got too close to my cat. It lacks useful features like automapping and spot-mow, and there are better options for the money above. The yellow finish is a bit garish for my tastes too.

EcoFlow Blade: While it was easy to set up and cut my lawn nicely without the need for any boundary wire, the EcoFlow Blade sometimes struggled with GPS navigation and ended up stuck in a flower bed. It also left an untouched strip around the edge of my lawn. The object avoidance was solid, and it can be automated in the app, though it occasionally failed to start a scheduled cut for me. EcoFlow seems to have discontinued this model, though it is still on sale in Europe. Probably best to avoid.

Yardcare E400: Curious about the budget end of the robot mower market, I agreed to try the Yardcare E400, but this mower was an unmitigated disaster from start to finish. It’s a boundary wire model, so you must run wire around the area you want mowed. Yardcare suggests it can cover up to 4,300 square feet and cut grass between 0.8 and 2.4 inches. The problem is that it gets stuck frequently and struggles to even get on and off its charging station reliably. After trying multiple fixes to no avail and going through customer support, I had to conclude that this model has a serious design flaw.

How Do Robot Lawn Mowers Work?

Perhaps counterintuitively, the setup instructions for your robot lawn mower will likely tell you to start by cutting the grass. Robot mowers mostly can’t deal with long grass. Unlike traditional mowers, these robots don’t collect grass cuttings; they mulch instead, and they are designed to cut frequently, keeping your lawn short and simply leaving the cuttings on the ground, which can also improve lawn health. Most robot mowers are designed to run two or three times a week during the growing season (from late spring to early fall).

They have rechargeable batteries onboard and can last from half an hour to several hours on a full charge. They return to the charging base and recharge automatically when their power runs low. Most mowers have simple controls, a small display, and an emergency stop button. You can generally start and stop mowing, set schedules, and create or edit mapped areas using the onboard controls or the companion mobile app, very much like a robot vacuum.

What Features Should I Look for in a Robot Mower?

There are many factors to consider in choosing a robot mower, and the best choice for you often depends on your yard.

Robot lawn mowers are generally rated to cover a specific square footage, with wider coverage requiring models with larger batteries. Alongside yard size, you should consider the shape and topography of your lawn, as most robot mowers will struggle with steep inclines. While you can often map out separate areas so your robot mower can mow front and back lawns, for example, it will generally need you to lift and carry it between those areas. If you have an uneven garden or steep slopes, look for a four-wheel-drive (4WD) or all-wheel-drive (AWD) mower and check the manufacturer's rating for inclines.

There are a few types of navigation that robot mowers employ. We’ve tested five different approaches, though some mowers combine multiple technologies for better performance.

  • Satellite: Often employing something called Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) Global Positioning System (GPS), these mowers need a satellite signal to navigate and will have a receiver that must be placed in the open with a clear line of sight to the sky. Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings.
  • Light Detection and Ranging (lidar): This technology sends out rapid laser pulses to 3D map the terrain (it is also used by self-driving cars). It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail.
  • Cameras: Cameras and onboard AI are used for obstacle detection and avoidance. AI vision can automatically map areas and cut the grass while avoiding obstacles it encounters, much like how most robot vacuums navigate a home to clean the floors.
  • Wire boundary: These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky.
  • Remote control: You mow your lawn from the comfort of your home using a remote controller or an app on your phone. Some only work via remote control, while others can also cut automatically.

Robot mowers generally come with large charging docks, and you’ll need to earmark a suitable spot for yours. They usually have extensive weatherproof cabling, but you will have to find a route to an outdoor socket.

To connect to your mower and schedule a mow, update the firmware, or remote control it where supported, you need a decent Wi-Fi signal or a Bluetooth connection. It’s best to set up your mower’s charging station within range of your Wi-Fi network. Some mowers also need a strong Wi-Fi signal to operate effectively, so you might consider adding an outdoor mesh router. If you want to connect your phone via Bluetooth, you will have to get quite close.

How Noisy Are Robot Mowers?

Most robot mowers are far quieter than their traditional counterparts. You can expect them to operate at around 55 decibels, though they may go as high as 75 decibels. We only tested battery-powered mowers, but expect gas mowers to be louder. While the operation is often quiet, I did find that several mowers made annoying beeping sounds when backing up or had a loud recorded voice during setup or upon receiving a command.

Do Robot Mowers Work in Any Weather?

Robot mowers and their charging stations usually have IP ratings and can cope with rain, but you should pack up and bring your mower indoors during the winter months. Many robot mowers have some kind of rain sensor and will pause mowing when it gets too wet. Some mowers may need to be paused manually. The wheels can churn up your lawn and get caked in mud if mowers continue to labor in the rain, especially with larger and heavier models.

How Well Do Robot Mowers Cut?

Mowers of different sizes will have varying cutting widths, denoting the width of the strip they can cut on each pass. Most also have floating cutting decks that enable you to choose the length of grass you want (typically 1 to 3 inches). Many robot mowers seem to struggle with cutting around the edges of a lawn, especially if there’s a wall or fence that prevents them from getting close enough.

It’s common to find an uncut verge around the edge of your lawn, so you might need to occasionally get the string trimmer out. Every robot mower I’ve tested has also struggled to cut the area around the charging station, so I recommend placing the unit on a deck or pavement if possible.

Can I Install a Robot Mower Myself?

​Yes, most robot mowers can be installed by anyone, but you might want to set aside an afternoon to work out any snags. Finding the best spot for the receiver for a satellite mower can be tricky. The mapping process can also take a while; usually, the mower will prompt you to remote-control it around the border you want to set. After the first mow, you should review its performance and make tweaks to ensure it’s covering the entire area you want to cut.

How I Test Robot Lawn Mowers

I test each robot lawn mower for at least a month, on at least two different lawn areas, assessing the ease of setup, the mapping process, automatic scheduling (where available), navigation, obstacle avoidance, and the quality of the final cut, looking for length, uniformity, and any missed patches. Where applicable, I try extra features, tweak settings in the app, and check how the mower handles different weather conditions. I also keep an eye on battery performance and charging time to ensure it aligns with the manufacturer's claims.

entries.title: Alienware 27 QD-OLED (AW2726DM) Review: A $350 Winner
entries.summary: We’ve come a long way since exclusively $1,000+ OLED gaming monitors. Alienware’s latest display brings the price down to a shocking $350, though it comes with some important compromises.
entries.content:
This type of QD-OLED arranges pixels in a way that’s different from LCD, which can cause issues when viewing small text. You may notice “color fringing” visible as an odd burst of green or purple filling the negative space between letters.

The AW2726DM just isn’t a sharp display, and it’s not great for viewing small text. As mentioned, it has a resolution of 2560 x 1440—or 1440p. This provides a pixel density of about 110 pixels per inch. By comparison, a standard 27-inch 4K monitor delivers about 165 pixels per inch.

However, sticking to 1440p feels like the right call for a monitor at this price point. As PC gamers likely know, increasing a game’s render resolution from 1440p to 4K comes with a huge performance penalty, and midrange GPUs struggle to handle demanding games at 4K.

Still, it’s QD-OLED, and all QD-OLED panels have two things going for them: Incredible contrast and superb color performance.

You might be familiar with OLED’s contrast advantage if you’ve bought a TV sometime this decade. OLED pixels are self-emissive, meaning the pixels themselves create light. That’s different from an LCD panel, which requires a backlight that shines through the pixels. OLED’s self-emissive technology provides a lot more control over how the image is lit, and the result is an image with far more contrast and depth than what LCD can achieve.

Samsung’s QD-OLED also uses quantum dots, a very cool tech that requires its own article to explain. Quantum dots generally provide great color, and the AW2726DM is no exception, as it reaches 98 percent of DCI-P3 and 94 percent of AdobeRGB. Those numbers are close to the top of what’s available from any monitor in 2026, regardless of price.

In the real world, the contrast and color translate to a vivid, realistic image with a sense of depth you won’t find from LCD alternatives. Games generally look colorful, rich, and alluring.

Brightness Gets the Boot

While the AW2726DM’s image quality is good, it makes one major sacrifice to achieve a lower price. It’s not very bright.

Alienware lists the AW2726DM’s maximum brightness at 200 nits. My review sample was just above that with a sustained maximum SDR brightness of 202 nits. For comparison, a more expensive OLED monitor (like the MSI MPG 271QR X50) can deliver 300 nits or more. I mostly used the monitor at about 60 percent of its maximum brightness, as the room where I view it doesn’t receive much direct sunlight. However, I had to up the brightness to 100 percent in peak afternoon sun if I left my curtains open.

The low SDR brightness has implications for HDR performance, too. The AW2726DM supports HDR, but it’s not VESA HDR–certified, and it promises just 400 nits of peak HDR brightness. In my testing, HDR brightness was no higher than SDR when the entire display was lit, and I recorded a maximum possible brightness of 398 nits when just 10 percent of the display was lit. For comparison, leading OLED monitors can deliver over 300 nits full-screen and over 1,000 nits in the 10 percent window. The AW2726DM can appear brighter in HDR than in SDR, but gamers who enjoy a lot of HDR titles will find the monitor underwhelming.

entries.title: People Are Ghosting Long-Term Partners. Some Don’t Regret It
entries.summary: The communication-free form of breaking up has become ubiquitous. “I no longer had to bear her energy,” a man who ghosted his partner of four years tells WIRED.
entries.content:
Dean met Nicole on Bumble in 2018, and they immediately bonded over their shared Chicago upbringing.

Nicole had kids, and they talked often about “wanting more than what we saw growing up in the environment we did,” Dean, a 37-year-old independent contractor, tells WIRED. They also both considered themselves more spiritual than religious, and were mentally, emotionally, and physically compatible. Best of all, “we rarely had a fight,” he says, “and could talk about any- and everything.”

They eventually moved in together and even talked about getting married, though he says the idea was one-sided. “She wanted to. I secretly didn't.”

In 2022, four years into the relationship, Dean says “she allowed her mind to be polluted” by “gender wars” discourse. As he saw it, she became one of those people who “attach themselves to feminism” and complained about men all the time. Even though Dean claims he is progressive, he says, “it wasn’t my thing” because Nicole had become overly negative.

It was around then that he started to get the ick. His mind was made up: Instead of talking to her about his frustrations, he blocked her phone number and social media accounts, one afternoon while she was at work.

In the months that followed, as Nicole attempted to get in contact with him through family members, Dean didn’t feel an ounce of remorse, only relief. “Like a weight was lifted off my shoulders. I no longer had to bear her energy.” (Citing privacy concerns, the ghosters WIRED spoke to for this story asked that they be identified by their first name only.)

Even now, he says he “absolutely” made the right decision.

With dating apps and social media determining so much of how people connect, ghosting—ending a relationship by ignoring or blocking the other person’s calls and texts, effectively icing them out—has become the breakup mode du jour.

According to a Thriving Center of Psychology survey, 84 percent of millennials and Gen Z say they’ve been ghosted at the end of a relationship. But while ghosting is widely accepted among singles during the initial stages of getting to know someone via the apps or as a means to end a situationship, it’s far less typical for multiyear relationships. In late June, Vogue UK shed light on the trend of “the disappearing boyfriend.” The article detailed the painful aftermath of women grappling with their partner’s sudden and shocking disappearance, noting how “many of these ghostings occur after things were seemingly going well.”

To address this new normal, Dating.com recently announced that it was hiring a “chief breakup officer” who, for $3,000 a month, would be tasked with ending other people’s relationships for them.

Naturally, ghosting is a lot easier when you’re communicating with strangers or people you know you’ll never run into again. When you know someone offline, there can be a greater sense of accountability, but even that doesn’t seem to always be the case anymore as expectations around communication are in decline.

In the r/ghosting subreddit, stories of long-term relationships ending when one person decided to completely vanish have become alarmingly common, as Redditors have tried to understand the psychology behind such abrupt and seemingly cruel detachment.

“I dated a girl for a year and a half. Out of the blue she said something in a normal discussion, and instead of having a conversation with her [about what upset me], I completely ignored her, walked away, refused to speak to her when she asked, and blocked her until she found out from someone else that we were done,” one commenter from r/ghosting tells WIRED over direct message.

Sumi, a 36-year-old resident of San Francisco, decided to abandon his 18-month relationship by ghosting his girlfriend. “I’ve been no-contact for about four weeks now,” he says.

Among Gen Z, terminating communication, romantic or otherwise, without any closure has become more pronounced. A recent survey by analytics firm Talker Research found that Gen Z are more likely to sever contact with a family member or loved one—60 percent—compared to older generations.

They often aestheticize estrangement by turning heartbreak into social content, as with the viral trend “I ghosted the [love of my life], trust me [I don’t give a fuck],” where young people pretend to act completely unfazed about former lovers by feigning extreme detachment. Some TikTokkers even added their own twists to the trend, posting about ghosting friends, parents, or their “entire bloodline” as a means of setting better boundaries.

“It’s important to keep in mind that Gen Z has grown up with dating apps and social media, so ghosting can seem like a normal part of the dating experience, even if it’s hurtful,” says Liesel Sharabi, an associate professor of communication at Arizona State University who specializes in the effect technology has on interpersonal relationships.

Sharabi adds that digital communication has made ghosting “easier and potentially more socially acceptable,” despite its harms. “We risk losing the humanity and decency we would want someone to show us when ending a relationship.”

There are ghosters who are emotionally immature, don’t take relationships seriously, or simply don't care about the impact they have on others. “But from an attachment perspective, I also see ghosting as a nervous system strategy,” says Becca Hansel, a Los Angeles–based therapist. Ghosters are often people with avoidant or disorganized attachment patterns, where “emotional closeness or conflict may start to feel threatening or overwhelming.”

For them, severing a relationship requires tolerating the discomfort of sitting with another person’s sadness or anger. But Hansel adds that some people who ghost aren’t doing it because they enjoy hurting the other person, even if it is an unhealthy coping strategy.

In some cases, ghosting is a means of escaping an abusive situation. “If someone doesn’t feel emotionally or physically safe, I don’t think they owe the other person an explanation,” Hansel says.

That’s what happened with Ashley, a 25-year-old education sales representative in Seattle. After nearly four years together she convinced herself that she didn’t want to feel the weight of breaking up with a boyfriend who started drinking a lot and became emotionally abusive. Instead of having a conversation about how everything went wrong, she ghosted him.

“I thought it would be easier for me to just disappear and for him to forget about it,” she tells WIRED. “He kept calling and texting me for quite a while after, for weeks, months, and years. And I just never ever picked up or responded again. I deleted all my social media accounts as well because I just didn't want to see any of it.”

Still, the difficult emotions often don't disappear even if ghosting is warranted. According to a 2025 study published in Computers in Human Behavior, ghosting has significant cognitive consequences for both parties involved, not just the victim. Compared to straightforward rejection, “the uncertainty and ambiguity inherent in ghosting” can create “more persistent adverse psychological effects” and prolong distress.

Ashley, who admits to having a pattern of avoiding difficult conversations in her life, says the decision still weighs on her. “I’d never broken up with someone in a really big relationship before, I had only been broken up with. Ghosting felt right at the time because I was scared of the outcome. It definitely wasn’t a great thing because it didn't do anything good for either of us. It still haunts me.”

Although she now believes people who get ghosted deserve an explanation “even if it hurts their feelings,” she never gave one to her ex, “and I don't think I ever will.”

Two years after they broke up, he had sex with Ashley’s then best friend, who later confessed about the hookup. “He did it to get back at me. So I won’t be talking to either of them ever again,” she says.

entries.title: The Best Audio Players for Kids: Yoto, Toniebox, and More
entries.summary: Whether you want an audio player that’ll grow with your kid or one that your toddler can operate independently, I have a recommendation for you.
entries.content:
In my current season of toddler parenthood, I’ve sometimes felt that I could cut the tension between myself and the TV remote with a knife. As much as I try to keep screen time in check, sometimes I need 10 uninterrupted minutes to unload the dishwasher before a certain almost-2-year-old goes for the dog bowl.

That’s where audio players are handy. In a world where screens are increasingly hard to avoid, parents are looking for alternatives—and these players, in their various formats, are to the rescue. The devices mark a sweet spot between independent play and story time, letting kids listen to music, audiobooks, and interactive stories without a tablet in sight. Some audio players are geared toward younger kiddos who enjoy tactile toys and familiar characters like Elmo and Bluey, while other options are designed to grow with them to chapter books, podcasts, and beyond.

Over the past several weeks, my family has tested some of the biggest names in the category to see how they stack up. Here’s the verdict on which ones are best suited for different families and their needs.

Want more recommendations for WIRED-tested kids’ toys? Here’s our guide to Brain-Boosting Toys for Kids, Kid-Approved STEM Toys, and the Best Gifts for Lego Lovers.

Best for Kids of All Ages

The Yoto Player is simple enough for toddlers to operate independently while offering a broad enough content library to keep it relevant as kids grow. Stories and music live on credit card–sized cards that my daughter could swap in and out with her little hands, and the small pixel display on the front of the machine adds a visual element without becoming another distracting screen.

You can add each Yoto card to your child’s library through the device’s companion app. Once you do, you can stream the content directly from your phone or remotely send it to the Yoto. That means you’re not necessarily tied to bringing the speaker with you everywhere you go. I saw this capability as being especially useful on road trips—you can play stories through your car speakers or listen from your phone if the player gets left behind or its battery dies.

Yoto offers more than the stories and songs from its player cards. You’ll also get kid-friendly daily radio, draw-alongs, toothbrush timers, white noise, a wake-up clock, and a nightlight that activates when you flip the player screen-side down. I only see it getting more useful as my daughter grows, and if I’m being honest, there is a Nancy Drew story collection I am secretly eyeing for myself.

My biggest concern is simply keeping track of all those little cards. I’ve found them tucked into couch cushions and hidden under rugs more than once. Sure, once a card is in your library, you can play it on the machine through the app, but that defeats the purpose of this being a “screen-free” device and one that my daughter can use independently. I also learned pretty quickly that the silicone Adventure Jacket accessory ($30) is more than a nice-to-have add-on after watching the machine take the occasional spill off the couch and my daughter carry it haphazardly from room to room.

Content format Cards
App Yoto app
Headphone jack? Yes
Power source Rechargeable via USB-C or magnetic dock
Extra features Podcasts, white noise, wake clock, night light, room thermometer

Best Bedtime Story Experience

This little device has become one of the most cherished parts of our bedtime routine. Every night, my husband and I climb into bed with our daughter, turn off the lights, and read together while casting the Moonlite projector. No longer is bedtime a fight; now all we have to do is say “story time,” and she grabs her milk, makes herself comfy in bed, and points at the ceiling.

More of a modern story projector than a traditional audio player, the Moonlite Storytime Projector is still relatively screen-free. The projector device clips over your phone’s flashlight and shines illustrations onto the opposite wall or the ceiling. Each story lives on a reel, and after scanning the reel’s QR code in the Moonlite app, it appears on your phone while the matching illustrations project in front of you. As you read, you manually advance the reel, like you’re operating a tiny film projector to “turn the page.”

It takes some practice to line up the projector with your phone’s flashlight and adjust the lens until the image is in focus, but the app walks you through this calibration process before every story starts. An adult still reads the stories, and the app provides optional sound effects and background music for extra immersion. Unlike the other products I tested, Moonlite isn’t meant to replace parent-led story time, but enhance it.

The trade-off here is that the Moonlite isn’t really something young kids can use independently. It relies entirely on a smartphone flashlight and the Moonlite app, so it’s a shared experience rather than an independent play activity. But if your goal is to create an engaging and fun bedtime ritual, I highly recommend it.

Content format Story reels
App Moonlite app
Headphone jack? N/A
Power source Uses your phone’s flashlight and battery
Extra features Sound effects, music, projected illustrations

Best for Character Lovers

Of all the kids’ audio players I tested, the Toniebox 2 was the easiest to pick up and understand. To operate the soft, cubed speaker, kids place a magnetic figurine on the top, and the associated stories and songs automatically play. The experience is very tactile; my daughter figured it out in minutes. She doesn’t know how Bluetooth works or what an audiobook is, but she absolutely understands that putting Cookie Monster on top of the Toniebox 2 means that Cookie Monster will start talking.

The accompanying app is nice, but it doesn’t feel essential. It sends push notifications when the speaker’s battery is running low; offers a listening recap, à la Spotify Wrapped; and includes a handful of free stories that don’t require purchasing additional Tonies, which add up quickly at around $15 to $20 for each figure. One of my favorite features is the ability to record your own voice reading stories, which I think will be great for the next time I have to spend a few nights away from my daughter. The Toniebox 2 also offers a sleep timer and sunrise alarm, though I haven’t tested these features for my daughter.

My grumbles with the whole Toniebox world are brief. I wish the figurines were labeled with the content they contain. Some characters represent specific movies or collections, and there’s no easy way to tell just by looking at them. For example, Bullseye and Jessie each hail from the Toy Story movie series, but the Bullseye Tonie focuses on Toy Story 5 content, and Jessie features only Toy Story 3 and 4. I always mix up the two figures. You can check the app for details on each Tonie, but I’d love a small identifier on each physical character. Also, the soft speaker is durable, but a built-in handle or carrying loop would make it much easier for my toddler to tote the device from room to room—especially because she’s usually double-fisting figurines at the same time. Even so, if your little one gravitates toward familiar characters, the Toniebox is one of the most intuitive audio players I’ve tested.

Content format Character figurines
App Tonies app
Headphone jack? Yes
Power source Rechargeable via USB-C
Extra features Sleep timer, sunrise alarm, app recap

Best Analog Option

After downloading apps, pairing devices, and scanning QR codes to get other audio players up and running, testing the simple Fisher-Price Rockin’ Record Player was a welcome breath of fresh air. All I had to do was put in batteries and it started playing, which felt satisfying and kind of nostalgic.

To operate this audio toy, kids place one of the chunky plastic “records” on the turntable, move the needle into place, and the music starts. Each record has a different theme—from country and hip hop to a wellness-inspired option—and includes two songs on each side. Some are classic nursery rhymes, and others are Fisher-Price originals. The records are easy to swap, and my daughter figured out how to operate the player by herself almost immediately.

My only real complaint—on behalf of my daughter—is the intentional record-scratch sound effect before each song. It’s a cute touch that sells the pretend record player experience, but each time she hears it, my daughter side-eyes me as if to say, “Well? Where’s the song?” The player is also bulky. That said, it pretty much permanently lives in the corner of my bathroom, where it keeps her entertained for long enough for me to get ready in the morning. With just two songs per side, the replay value is not huge and depends on how many record packs you collect. But if you’re looking for a simple music player that works without you needing to download another app, this player is hard not to love.

Content format Plastic records
App N/A
Headphone jack? No
Power source AA batteries
Extra features N/A

entries.title: The Delicate Art of Making a 1907 House Smarter
entries.summary: I tested modern locks, lights, climate controls, and more in a historic home that I very much wanted to keep historic.
entries.content:
At the very end of 2025, my wife and I bought our first home, a 1907 Craftsman in the heart of Portland, Oregon. It’s a beautiful old house, listed on the National Historic Registry, and is largely unchanged from the day it was built. This is exactly what we dreamed of in a house. It’s loaded with history and vibes, mostly unmessed with across the decades. We’re now simultaneously updating and restoring the home with a limited budget, big ideas, our own style, and plenty of sweat equity.

The place we moved into was the level opposite of a “smart home”—and figuring out thoughtful ways to integrate modern technology into this old house without sacrificing aesthetics or ruining the vibe is the guiding principle.

We’re only getting started, but after a busy six months of learning, researching, and working cutting-edge technology into a house from the Roosevelt administration (Teddy, not FDR), I’ve kept a running log of the tech choices we’ve made along the way. Today, our house is starting to feel simultaneously old and new, which is very much the goal. It’s a lot of work, but I assure you it’s also a wonderful time.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

A Smart Thermostat

Replacing the home’s heating system was a day one fix—our furnace was kicking off carbon monoxide and needed to be addressed immediately. We had a local furnace company in the basement before even moving in. But for daily use, we paired our spiffy new furnace with Ecobee’s new, midrange Ecobee Enhanced smart thermostat, which has a larger touchscreen than the basic Essential model and built-in radar for motion detection.

In making this choice, I consulted WIRED’s in-depth review of the Ecobee, which prioritizes the unit’s ease of setup and intuitive interface—this made a strong case for selecting the Ecobee over other similar smart thermostats, like the Google Nest, which lacks the Ecobee’s presence sensors.

The Ecobee gives us a monthly recap of our furnace usage and the average temperature in our home; walking into a low home-energy-score environment in a home that lacks insulation and gets drafty, having this monthly recap has been helpful already. Many states have a smart thermostat rebate program through local gas and power companies, and right now we’re earning around $10 off each monthly bill for having a smart thermostat in the house.

The Ecobee sits unobtrusively in our dining room; I’ve toyed with adding a vintage-leaning thermostat backing plate into the mix (Atomic Surplus makes really cool ones), though most of these are more midcentury than early 20th century. For now, a pop of digital in our old dining room doesn’t look too out of place.

A Smart Air Conditioner for Older Windows

Installing a proper whole-home air conditioning system into our home—which had never been done before—proved dauntingly cost-prohibitive as a day one update. And so instead we’ve opted to go with a couple of these excellent smart units from Midea, whose products install into any standard-sized window and simultaneously cool, dehumidify, and ventilate.

These are perfect for the two working bedrooms in our home: They are whisper-quiet because the condenser part of the unit is actually outside, and the unit’s U-shaped design makes it so you only have to have your window open around six inches to install, as opposed to the normal 20 inches of most traditional window air conditioners. Our windows are very old and don’t open all the way—this makes the Midea’s U-shape especially helpful, and guided our decision to select this unit.

The Midea’s app functionality is really nice. You can put your airflow on a schedule, and it can be turned on and off remotely, a function that we used with great relish on the drive home from a recent camping trip. It has a clever sleep function as well, which lets you set the room colder as you’re falling asleep, then warming things up as the ambient temperature cools outside over the course of the night. Plus the filter is easy to access and clean.

At some point we will likely upgrade the air cooling system for the whole house, but these Midea units have made it possible to delay that choice without sacrificing comfort in our sleeping space.

A Smart Lock That Doesn’t Require Hardwiring

I don’t want to make it sound as if our front door was held together by rusted chicken wire upon moving in, but it wasn’t far off. Addressing the door locks was a top-line need, and this system by Philips checked every box.

Efficient, affordable, and smart, these locks remove the need for bulky jangling keys (the bête noir of our rental days) and replaced them with an all-in-one unit that connects to our Wi-Fi, uses our unique fingerprints for entry, and can be easily updated with one-time codes for guests, the occasional pet-sitter, and so forth.

There are many smart home locks on the market, and WIRED’s guide features several great choices, but the Philips 4200 does not require its own “hub,” dongle, or additional apparatus in order to start working immediately. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are built into the 4200, which runs on batteries and doesn’t need to be hardwired. And the all-in-one nature of the 4200 helps keep things smartly priced: The entire unit is available for around $120, with no additional products or subscriptions required to do its thing.

Perhaps you’ve encountered a smart lock like this during an Airbnb stay, but having it on the door of your home is kind of a game changer. It’s simplified a step of our life, and allowed our kid to have the autonomy to come and go from our home without needing to bring along her own keys. To me, this is emblematic smart-home tech: subtle, effective, and unobtrusive. I will never have to drive back home again at the start of a road trip to make sure the door is locked, because now I can just check the app. (It was already locked anyway.)

A 21st Century Bidet

The toilets in our home had been updated (at some point in the ’70s), but left much to be desired. Happily for all involved, shortly after moving in I undertook a comprehensive overhaul of WIRED’s authoritative guide to bidet technology. The glimmering jewel of all that good-natured buttmaxxing was an opportunity to install the Toto Aurora Washlet+ 7A with Integrativity System, which is without qualm or peer the nicest toilet I have ever experienced.

This mighty throne seamlessly integrates Toto’s universally well-regarded S7A bidet, providing automatic seat lifting and lowering and auto-flush. When paired together, these functions let you use your toilet without ever touching a button. The nozzle, heated seat, air dry, and oscillation capabilities are outstanding. You can also pair oscillation with a pulse action on the S7A for a noticeably more thorough experience.

I went ahead and hired a plumber for this installation, and he helped me navigate some of the quirks involved in putting a brand new high-tech unit into ancient pipes—in particular, the distance from the back wall to the toilet flange required a different size of “rough-in” than what comes standard from Toto. I also had to install a new electrical outlet near the toilet, which involved hiring an electrician.

But my goodness, was it all worth it. The innovative Integravity System cleans and refreshes the toilet each time you flush. Toto calls this “dual phase cleaning,” which reduces the time between flushing and rinsing to ensure the bowl sparkles after every use. It also only uses one gallon of water per flush, which is well below the Environmental Protection Agency standard of 1.6 gallons per flush.

Now the primary upstairs bathroom in which it sits is subtly perhaps the nicest and most complete room in the entire house. Does the Toto S7A “look vintage” in any way? No. Frankly, I think a person in 1907 would be positively astonished by the experience of using this technology, which is a funny thing to ponder. But our goal is to create a home that feels simultaneously old and new at the same time, and accepting compromises along the way. With this in mind, the S7A feels essential; something about its sleek, modern form creates a sort of pleasing aesthetic friction in our old house, particularly in the updated 1970s bathroom in which it resides.

Smart Lighting

The house I’m working with is an outdated mystery of coiled electrical systems, and someday we’ll need to fully unspool the mystery. But for getting started on actually living in the place, a combination of smart lighting and ambient lighting solutions has made a huge difference in the home. I’m convinced lighting is one of the most important things we can do to make inhabited environments more comfortable, especially if you’ll be working from home.

Feit Electric makes an outstanding smart light bulb, which we’ve used to retrofit vintage light fixtures in a room without an overhead light. It allows us to put the lights on a timer, and can be controlled from its own app. You can also pair these lights with an Alexa or other smart home management system, and we’ve got that set up in our kid’s bedroom, which lets her use voice commands to turn the lights on and off in her room. You can adjust the brightness and hue easily using the app, and installation was effortless.

We’ve also been very happy with the Bluetooth light system by Zoiinet, which in our primary bedroom we have set up to provide overhead lighting. This is kind of the ultimate old house hack—rather than rewiring the room to add in overhead lighting (the bedrooms only came with wall mounts), we were able to install this socket without needing to hire an electrician. The socket is coupled with a touch switch, which we have installed on our wall, just like a normal wall switch. Set this up, and Bob’s your uncle—you’ve installed overhead lighting in your old house with weird electrical needs, all without having to get into the electrical system at all.

For Keeping Old Floors Spic-and-Span

I’ve talked a bit in this story about my spouse and our kid, but there is another, no less crucial member of the family whose life has been improved by the implementation of smart tech into our new home. Her name is Jojo, and she’s a rescue cat from the Oregon Humane Society. Gray with a white tummy (the best variety of cat), Jojo is particular when it comes to cleanliness, going so far as to drop the occasional protest deuce outside of her litter box if it’s not kept up to immaculate standards.

Such concerns have been forever ameliorated by an automatic litter box. Specifically, WIRED’s pick for Best AI-Enabled Automatic Litter Box, Whisker’s top-line Litter-Robot 5 Pro. It’s by far the best litter box I have ever had the pleasure of owning after a lifetime of cat ownership.

Jojo took to the unit without any issue, and my wife and I appreciate the robot’s notifications about functionality, particularly with regards to how full the waste bin is, and when it next needs changing. The LR5 gives us regular data about our cat, and I think if you’re even slightly sort of a cat person, it’s nice knowing that your cat is regularly using the bathroom and behaving itself.

The box does a frankly incredible job of not smelling—the “Advanced Odor Control” actually distinguishes between what, precisely, Jojo is up to in there, and uses the robot’s tech accordingly. We keep the unit in our laundry room, on the same floor as our bedroom spaces, and I’ve never caught an unpleasant whiff from its general direction, ever.

Ultimately, the most important aesthetic consideration around why we like the LR5 is its relative unobtrusiveness: It disappears into the corner of our laundry room, and when it comes to litter boxes, that’s perhaps the highest compliment of all. Consult this guide, talk to your vet, book a pet psychic, and go with your gut. Our cat loves it. We love it. It’s a game-changer.

A Retro Vacuum

Having a really cute vacuum cleaner makes vacuuming—an otherwise boring chore that simply has to be done, especially with kids and pets—an altogether more delightful experience. There are a growing number of quite modern vacuum options out there on the market, but I was drawn to these charmingly retro “Rosey the Robot”-looking models from Sebo, a German brand.

Both the Felix and Automatic models are lovely enough to be left out or tucked into a corner—these are vacuum cleaners so attractive you’ll feel bad about sticking them in your closet, and in an old house like ours, closet space is already at a high premium. And they work great, with multi-brush agitation modes, hospital-grade filtration, exhaust filters, and a heavy-duty belt with lifetime warranty. I think most vacuum cleaners operate with an “out of sight, out of mind” mentality, but these are both charming to look at, and letting them be out as part of our house is quite lovely.

A Smart Sprinkler for the Yard

Maybe the coolest thing about our house is the yard, a jewel-box quarter acre on the corner of our lot. It was more or less in a state of disrepair when we took over, blanketed in a thick layer of English ivy (vile weed), badly in need of arboreal trimming and care, and totally unmanaged in terms of water flow and irrigation.

I personally undertook the first huge tranche of work on this project: yanking out around 40 Home Depot garbage bags worth of the cursed ivy by the roots, reviving the dead soil by way of “the lasagna method” (Patricia Lanza’s book was a crucial housewarming gift from my mother-in-law), and then replanting most of the yard using a wild meadow mix from Northwest Meadowscapes. A few months later, I’m happy to report we have blooms, the bugs and birds have returned, and we’re able to start dreaming about what might come next.

Crucial to the meadow planting process has been the use of an OtO smart sprinkler, a movable automatic watering unit that sets up via app and can be placed strategically around the yard. This is ideal for a large yard lot, which presents a series of irrigation challenges; someday we may upgrade to an in-ground system, but for now we consulted WIRED’s guide to smart sprinklers and went with reviewer Christopher Null’s qualified recommendation around OtO: pint-sized, intelligent, and solar-powered, with only a garden hose required to get started.

“Most smart sprinklers are really smart controllers that need an in-ground system already in place,” says Brit Sastrawidjaya of Blueprint Earth, an ecological landscape designer based in Oregon, who confirmed the utility of the OtO for a new garden. “A smart hose timer just runs one setting wherever you set the sprinkler down. OtO lets you set different zones from one spot, and that matters, because every part of a garden waters differently while it's establishing.”

The app is fairly simple to use; programming the watering area had a slight learning curve and required some adjustment and experimentation to find what worked best, but as the yard has grown it’s been intuitive to further dial in the system and continue adjusting parameters. OtO allows you to set a watering schedule, turn the sprinkler on and off remotely, and set the depth of water you’d like to achieve.

We’ve supplemented OtO with hand watering, especially on hot days, but for the most part, OtO is handling our watering needs beautifully so far. Best of all, the OtO’s built-in solar panel is great—we’ve left it unplugged all summer after a single full charge to get things started.

A Fancy Faucet System

The infamous kitchen remodel: slayer of finances, bane of relationships, the final frontier of home project Valhalla. Our kitchen is the only part of the house that’s been even slightly updated in the last hundred years, and it’s awful: We’re talking full demo territory, new cabinets, new everything.

There’s miles to go on this kitchen project, which is a double-your-pleasure, double-your-expenses-style situation due to the fact that an awkwardly placed bathroom lurks in the back corner of our current kitchen layout. Thus far we’ve started with the Aquifier 4-in-1 faucet system, which comes with filtered, hot, and sparkling water options. It’s simple and intuitive to use, with an easy install—it even comes with a refillable C02 cartridge.

The finishes are beautiful and timeless, and a tall faucet is especially conducive if your spouse or partner loves and collects various sizes and styles of water bottles—we’ve been using this every day for this exact purpose, and the sparkling water attachment is already saving me money on restocking La Croix. This may be the easiest thing I do on this kitchen remodel project, which, I fear, is going to be a long road ahead.
